about: The criteria a project is judged against. Each has a minimum risk tier from which it is mandatory, an optional condition (it applies only to projects with that feature), and the lowest evidence grade that can support a 'meets' result. Grades: A = the reviewer ran, reproduced or measured it; B = the reviewer inspected the thing itself (code, configuration, the document being judged); C = a statement only (documentation, the author's word).

features.aiAssisted: AI coding agents or assistants write or change the code
features.personalData: stores personal data (names, emails, addresses, messages, health, financial)
features.money: takes payments, issues refunds or credits, or holds balances
features.limitedStock: sells or allocates something limited (stock, seats, coupons, slots)
features.browserDatabase: the browser talks to the database directly (Supabase, Firebase and similar)
features.ai: calls an AI model at runtime
features.launchSpike: expects a launch, promotion or other traffic spike

areas.name: Reviewability
areas.question: Can a reviewer start work from the README alone?

areas.name: Harness
areas.question: Will the next change, by a person or an AI agent, keep the project correct?

areas.name: Architecture
areas.question: Is the structure sound for the agreed requirements?

areas.name: Security
areas.question: Who can do what, and can anything leak?

areas.name: Performance
areas.question: Will it hold the expected traffic and stay correct?

areas.name: Operations
areas.question: Will we see problems, and can we recover?

areas.name: Quality history
areas.question: What has gone wrong before, and is it fixed for good?

areas.name: Acceptance and report
areas.question: Does it do what we agreed, and can the owner understand the result?

criteria.title: Purpose is stated
criteria.standard: The README says in plain words what the product does, who uses it and which user journeys matter most.
criteria.evidence: The README.

checks.q: Does the README say in plain words what the product does?
Does it say who uses it?
Does it name the user journeys that matter most?

criteria.title: Runs from a clean checkout
criteria.standard: Following only the README, a reviewer gets the app running locally or on a staging copy within 30 minutes. No undocumented steps.
criteria.evidence: The reviewer's own run: commands and output.

checks.q: Following only the README on a clean checkout, did the app start?
Did it start within 30 minutes?
Was every step needed written in the README?

criteria.title: Review page is complete
criteria.standard: A review page in this standard's format exists, is linked from the README, and passes the validator for the submission stage.
criteria.evidence: Validator output.

checks.q: Is there a review pack in this standard's format?
Does the README link to the review page?
Does `review-pack.mjs gate submission` pass on it?

criteria.title: Every setting is documented
criteria.standard: Every setting the app reads is listed with its purpose, whether it is secret, an example value and whether production needs it.
criteria.evidence: The settings table compared with a search of the code for every setting it reads.

checks.q: Is every setting the code reads listed (checked against a search of the code)?
Does each listed setting give its purpose, whether it is secret, an example and whether production needs it?

criteria.title: Test access is ready
criteria.standard: Test accounts for every role and a way to reset test data are documented. Payments, email and other side effects run in test mode.
criteria.evidence: The reviewer used the accounts and the reset.

checks.q: Are there test accounts, or a documented way to create them, for every role?
Is there a documented way to reset test data?
Do payments, email and other side effects run in test mode?

criteria.title: A staging copy exists
criteria.standard: A staging environment, separate from production with its own database and keys, is available to the reviewer.
criteria.evidence: Staging address and its configuration.

checks.q: Is a staging copy available to the reviewer?
Does staging have its own database and keys, separate from production?

criteria.title: Requirements are agreed
criteria.standard: The requirements the review judges against are written down with numbers (traffic, response times, acceptable data loss, recovery time) and agreed by a named person.
criteria.evidence: The requirements section, with who agreed and when.

checks.q: Are the traffic and response-time targets written down with numbers?
Are the acceptable data loss and recovery time written down with numbers?
Did a named person agree them, with a date?

criteria.title: Known limits are declared
criteria.standard: The author lists known problems, limitations and what is out of scope.
criteria.evidence: Known problems register and out-of-scope list.

checks.q: Is there a list of known problems?
Is what is out of scope listed?

criteria.title: Versions are pinned
criteria.standard: Runtime and tool versions are stated, and dependency lockfiles are committed.
criteria.evidence: README, version files, lockfiles.

checks.q: Are the runtime and tool versions stated?
Are dependency lockfiles committed?

criteria.title: Agent instructions exist
criteria.standard: An instruction file at the root (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or equivalent) tells coding agents how to set up, build, test and run the project.
criteria.evidence: The file.
criteria.source: agents.md format; Claude Code memory files

checks.q: Is there an agent instruction file (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or similar) at the root?
Does it say how to set up, test and run the project?

criteria.title: Agent instructions are true
criteria.standard: Every command in the instruction file works as written, and every path and rule it mentions matches the code.
criteria.evidence: The reviewer ran each command.

checks.q: Does every command in the instruction file work as written?
Does every path and rule it mentions match the code?

criteria.title: Agents know the rules and boundaries
criteria.standard: The instruction file states the rules that must never be broken (the business rules, where money and secrets are handled, files never edited by hand such as applied migrations) and the module boundaries.
criteria.evidence: The file compared with the business rules section.

checks.q: Does it state the business rules that must never be broken?
Does it say where money and secrets are handled?
Does it name the files never edited by hand and the module boundaries?

criteria.title: Lessons are recorded for agents
criteria.standard: Each recurring problem from the quality history appears in the instruction file as a short rule, linked to the test or check that enforces it.
criteria.evidence: The file compared with the recurring problems.

checks.q: Is every recurring problem from the quality history in it as a short rule?
Does each of those rules point to the test or check that enforces it?

criteria.title: Agent instructions are lean and safe
criteria.standard: The instruction file is short enough to be read in full every time (details linked out), contains no secrets and doesn't contradict itself or the code.
criteria.evidence: The file.

checks.q: Can it be read in full in a few minutes, with details linked out?
Is it free of secrets?
Is it free of contradictions, with itself and with the code?

criteria.title: Every promise has a test
criteria.standard: Every Must acceptance criterion and every business rule has an automated test.
criteria.evidence: A table from each criterion and rule to its test.

checks.q: Does every Must acceptance criterion have an automated test?
Does every business rule have an automated test?

criteria.title: Tests check outcomes
criteria.standard: Tests assert the business result (stock, balance, order state, what the user sees, including what should disappear), not only status codes or that a page loaded.
criteria.evidence: A sample of tests.

checks.q: Do the tests check the business result (stock, money, order state), not only status codes or that a page loaded?
Do the browser tests also check what should disappear?

criteria.title: Failure paths are tested
criteria.standard: Tests cover malformed and invalid input, unauthorised access, double submission, restarts, timeouts and slow or failing partners, not only the happy path.
criteria.evidence: The test list, by failure type.

checks.q: Is there an automated test with malformed and invalid input?
Is there an automated test of access by the wrong user and by nobody?
Is there an automated test of a double submission?
Is there an automated test of a restart?
Is there an automated test with a slow or failing partner?

criteria.title: Tests are reliable
criteria.standard: The whole suite passes three runs in a row with retries turned off.
criteria.evidence: Three run logs.

checks.q: Did the whole suite pass three runs in a row with retries turned off?

criteria.title: Every change goes through CI
criteria.standard: Tests and checks run automatically on every change, and the main branch accepts only changes that pass.
criteria.evidence: CI configuration and recent runs, branch protection.

checks.q: Do the tests run automatically on every change (CI)?
Does the main branch accept only changes that pass?

criteria.title: Lint and type checks pass
criteria.standard: A linter or formatter and, where the language has one, a type checker are configured and pass.
criteria.evidence: The reviewer's run.

checks.q: Is a linter or formatter configured, and does it pass?
Where the language has one, is a type checker configured, and does it pass?

criteria.title: Security checks are automated
criteria.standard: Secret scanning and vulnerable-dependency checks run in CI or before every commit.
criteria.evidence: CI configuration or hooks, and a recent run.

checks.q: Does secret scanning run in CI or before every commit?
Does a vulnerable-dependency check run in CI or before every commit?

criteria.title: Changes get an independent review
criteria.standard: Changes, AI-generated ones included, are reviewed before merging by someone other than their author: a person or a separate agent session.
criteria.evidence: Recent pull requests and their reviews.

checks.q: Is every change reviewed before merging by someone other than its author (a person or a separate agent session)?

criteria.title: The system map is complete
criteria.standard: Every entry point (pages, APIs, webhooks, scheduled jobs, admin and test routes, browser-to-database access) is listed with who may call it and what it touches. The reviewer found none missing.
criteria.evidence: The map compared with the code's routes and jobs.

checks.q: Is every entry point listed (pages, APIs, webhooks, scheduled jobs, admin and test routes, browser-to-database access), with none missing when compared with the code?
Does each say who may call it and what it touches?

criteria.title: Responsibilities are clear
criteria.standard: Each component has one stated job. Business rules live in one place on the server, not repeated in the browser or across services.
criteria.evidence: Component list and the code behind each rule.

checks.q: Does each component have one stated job?
Does each business rule live in one place on the server, not repeated in the browser or across services?

criteria.title: Decisions are recorded
criteria.standard: Major design choices (database, hosting, payments, where state is kept) are written down with the reason, the alternatives and the known downsides.
criteria.evidence: Decision records.

checks.q: Are the major design choices (database, hosting, payments, where state is kept) written down?
Does each give the reason, the alternatives and the downsides?

criteria.title: Outside calls are bounded
criteria.standard: Every call to another service has a timeout, limited retries with back-off, and a defined outcome when it fails or doesn't answer.
criteria.evidence: The code for each outside call.

checks.q: Does every call to another service have a time limit?
Are retries limited, with back-off?
Is there a defined outcome when the service fails or doesn't answer?

criteria.title: Slow work is off the request path
criteria.standard: Email, file processing, reports and similar work run in the background through a durable queue or outbox, so a slow partner doesn't slow the user.
criteria.evidence: The code path for each slow task.

checks.q: Does slow work (email, files, reports) run outside the user's request?
Is that work kept in a durable queue or outbox, so it survives a restart?

criteria.title: Scales out, or states its limit
criteria.standard: App servers keep nothing in their own memory that must be shared or survive (sessions, counters, rate limits, queues), or the one-server limit is documented and accepted.
criteria.evidence: In-memory state found in the code, and the decision record.

checks.q: Is state that must be shared or survive (sessions, counters, rate limits, queues) kept outside the app server's memory, or is the one-server limit written down and accepted?

criteria.title: Environments are separated
criteria.standard: Development, staging and production use separate databases, keys and accounts.
criteria.evidence: Configuration per environment.

checks.q: Does production have its own database, separate from development and testing?
Does production have its own keys and accounts?

criteria.title: Configuration is safe
criteria.standard: Settings come from the environment, not the code. Production refuses to start with missing, placeholder or test settings.
criteria.evidence: A start attempt with bad settings.

checks.q: Do settings come from the environment rather than the code?
Does production refuse to start with missing, placeholder or test settings?

criteria.title: Launch settings have one source of truth
criteria.standard: Values that must be right on the day (opening times, prices, stock, switches) are set in one place, parsed strictly (full date, time and time zone), and the value in force is visible.
criteria.evidence: Change the setting, restart, and read the value in force.

checks.q: Is each value that must be right on the day (opening time, price, stock, switches) set in one place only?
Is it read strictly (full date, time and time zone; anything else refused)?
Can the value in force be seen?

criteria.title: Database changes are versioned
criteria.standard: Schema changes run through versioned migrations. Nothing deletes data at start-up. Destructive changes have a backup and a plan.
criteria.evidence: Migrations and start-up code.

checks.q: Do schema changes run through versioned migrations?
Does nothing delete data at start-up?
Do destructive changes have a backup and a plan?

criteria.title: Dependencies are real and needed
criteria.standard: Every dependency exists in the official registry under that exact name, is maintained, and is needed.
criteria.evidence: Dependency list checked against the registry.
criteria.source: OWASP Top 10:2025 A03 Software Supply Chain Failures

checks.q: Does every dependency exist in the official registry under that exact name?
Is every dependency maintained and needed?

criteria.title: Partner limits are known
criteria.standard: Rate limits, quotas and costs of each outside service are known and fit the expected peak.
criteria.evidence: Provider documentation compared with the target load.

checks.q: Are the rate limits, quotas and costs of each outside service known?
Do they fit the expected peak?

criteria.title: Business rules are written down
criteria.standard: The business rules are listed in plain words, for example "never sell more than the stock", "one per customer", "every paid order has exactly one payment".
criteria.evidence: The business rules section.

checks.q: Are the business rules written down in plain words?

criteria.title: Rules can't be bypassed
criteria.standard: Each rule is enforced where it can't be skipped: a database constraint, a transaction or an atomic update. A check followed by a separate write does not count.
criteria.evidence: Schema and code for each rule.

checks.q: Is each business rule enforced where it can't be skipped (a database constraint, a transaction or an atomic update, not a check followed by a separate write)?

criteria.title: The server decides prices and permissions
criteria.standard: Prices, totals, discounts, roles and ownership are worked out on the server from trusted data, never taken from the browser.
criteria.evidence: The code, and a tampered request.

checks.q: Are prices, totals and discounts worked out on the server from trusted data?
Are roles and ownership worked out on the server, never taken from the browser?

criteria.title: Money is exact
criteria.standard: Amounts are stored as whole minor units (cents) or a decimal type. Rounding and currency rules are stated.
criteria.evidence: Schema and calculations.

checks.q: Are amounts stored as whole minor units (cents) or a decimal type?
Are rounding and currency rules stated?

criteria.title: Repeats are safe
criteria.standard: Creating orders, charges and other one-off actions is idempotent: a double click, a retry or a replayed request never creates a second one.
criteria.evidence: A double-submit and a retry test.

checks.q: Does a double click create only one order and one charge?
Does a retried or replayed request create no second order or charge?

criteria.title: Steps that belong together complete together
criteria.standard: Steps that belong together (reserve, charge, record) all happen, or are undone or completed by a recovery path. Money never moves without a record.
criteria.evidence: The code path and a test that interrupts it.

checks.q: If the process stops between charging and recording, is the purchase completed or undone by a recovery path, so money never moves without a record?

criteria.title: Unknown outcomes are settled
criteria.standard: When a payment or other outside action times out, the outcome is treated as unknown, not failed, and a background job settles it with the provider.
criteria.evidence: A slow-partner test.

checks.q: Is a time-out of a payment or other outside action treated as unknown, not failed?
Does a background job settle unknown outcomes with the provider?

criteria.title: Input is validated at the edge
criteria.standard: Every input is checked for type, range, length and format, and rejected rather than silently corrected. Malformed requests get a 4xx answer, never a crash.
criteria.evidence: Malformed requests sent by the reviewer.
criteria.source: OWASP Top 10:2025 A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions

checks.q: Is every input checked for type, range, length and format?
Do malformed requests get a 4xx answer, never a crash?
Is bad input rejected rather than silently corrected?

criteria.title: Time is handled explicitly
criteria.standard: Times are stored in UTC. Business times (opening hours, deadlines) carry a time zone. Date parsing is strict.
criteria.evidence: Code, and attempts with ambiguous dates.

checks.q: Are times stored in UTC?
Do business times (opening hours, deadlines) carry a time zone?
Are ambiguous dates refused?

criteria.title: Changes leave an audit trail
criteria.standard: Changes to money, stock and admin settings record who, what and when.
criteria.evidence: Logs or audit table after an admin change.

checks.q: Do changes to money, stock and admin settings record who, what and when?

criteria.title: Personal data has a lifecycle
criteria.standard: What personal data is kept, why, for how long, and how it is deleted on request is stated and implemented.
criteria.evidence: Privacy notes and the deletion path.

checks.q: Is it stated what personal data is kept, why and for how long?
Is there a working way to delete a person's data on request?

criteria.title: Records are reconciled
criteria.standard: A routine check compares records with reality (charges with orders, stock with sales) and alerts on any difference.
criteria.evidence: The check, run once.

checks.q: Is there a routine check comparing records with reality (charges with orders, stock with sales)?
Does a difference raise an alert?

criteria.title: Real payments work end to end
criteria.standard: The real payment flow has been exercised with the real provider: a purchase, a decline and a refund in the provider's test mode, and one small real purchase and refund in production before launch.
criteria.evidence: The provider's records of those transactions, matched to the app's orders.

checks.q: Have a purchase, a decline and a refund been made in the real provider's test mode?
Is one small real purchase and refund done, or planned before launch, in production?

criteria.title: No secrets are exposed
criteria.standard: No secrets in the code, git history, logs or anything sent to the browser.
criteria.evidence: Secret scan of files and history, and of the browser bundle.

checks.q: Are the code and git history free of secrets (secret scan)?
Is everything sent to the browser free of secrets?
Are logs free of secrets?

criteria.title: Every entry point checks who is asking
criteria.standard: Identity and ownership are checked on the server at every entry point. Nobody can read or change another user's data by changing an id.
criteria.evidence: Requests as another user and as nobody.
criteria.source: OWASP Top 10:2025 A01 Broken Access Control

checks.q: Does every entry point check on the server who is asking?
Is it impossible to read or change another user's data by changing an id?

criteria.title: Admin and test routes are closed
criteria.standard: Admin functions need an admin role with personal accounts, not a shared password. Test, debug and seed routes don't exist in production.
criteria.evidence: Requests to every admin and test route.

checks.q: Do admin functions need an admin role?
Do admins have personal accounts rather than a shared password?
Are test, debug and seed routes absent from production?

criteria.title: Database rules deny by default
criteria.standard: Where the browser talks to the database directly, access rules deny by default and are tested for each table.
criteria.evidence: Rules file and test queries with the public key.

checks.q: Do the database access rules deny by default?
Is each table's access tested with the public key?

criteria.title: No injection
criteria.standard: Database queries are parameterised. No shell command, template or HTML is built from user input without encoding.
criteria.evidence: Code scan and review.

checks.q: Are all database queries parameterised?
Is no shell command, template or HTML built from user input without encoding?

criteria.title: Sign-in is done properly
criteria.standard: Sign-in uses a proven provider or library. Passwords are hashed with a slow algorithm. Session cookies are Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite. Signing out ends the session.
criteria.evidence: Code and a sign-in session.

checks.q: Does sign-in use a proven provider or library?
Are passwords, if any, hashed with a slow algorithm?
Are session cookies Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite?
Does signing out end the session?

criteria.title: Abuse is limited
criteria.standard: Sign-in, sign-up, password reset, checkout and other costly endpoints have rate limits or bot protection.
criteria.evidence: Repeated requests until the limit applies.

checks.q: Do sign-in, sign-up and password reset have rate limits or bot protection?
Do checkout and other costly endpoints have rate limits or bot protection?

criteria.title: Safe defaults on the wire
criteria.standard: HTTPS everywhere, security headers set, cross-site access (CORS) limited to known sites.
criteria.evidence: Header check against the running site.

checks.q: Is HTTPS used everywhere?
Are security headers set?
Is cross-site access (CORS) limited to known sites?

criteria.title: Errors don't leak internals
criteria.standard: Users never see stack traces, SQL or internal paths.
criteria.evidence: Requests that cause errors.

checks.q: Do error answers hide stack traces, SQL and internal paths?

criteria.title: No known exploitable vulnerabilities
criteria.standard: Dependencies are scanned for known vulnerabilities and every hit is triaged.
criteria.evidence: Dependency scan output and triage notes.
criteria.source: OWASP Top 10:2025 A03 Software Supply Chain Failures

checks.q: Were the dependencies scanned for known vulnerabilities?
Was every hit triaged?

criteria.title: Webhooks are verified
criteria.standard: Incoming webhooks check the sender's signature and ignore replays.
criteria.evidence: A forged and a replayed webhook.

checks.q: Does every incoming webhook check the sender's signature?
Are replayed webhooks ignored?

criteria.title: Uploads are contained
criteria.standard: Uploaded files are checked for type and size, stored outside the web root and served safely.
criteria.evidence: Upload attempts with bad files.

checks.q: Are uploads checked for type and size?
Are they stored outside the web root and served safely?

criteria.title: AI features are fenced
criteria.standard: Features that call an AI model resist prompt injection, can't reveal other users' data, and have cost and rate limits.
criteria.evidence: Injection attempts and the limits in code.

checks.q: Do the AI features resist prompt injection when tried?
Are they unable to reveal other users' data?
Do they have cost and rate limits?

criteria.title: Personal data is protected
criteria.standard: Personal data is kept to what is needed, travels only over encrypted connections, and stays out of logs and error reports.
criteria.evidence: Logs from a test run, and the data model.

checks.q: Is personal data kept to what is needed?
Does it travel only over encrypted connections?
Does it stay out of logs and error reports?

criteria.title: An independent security test is booked
criteria.standard: An independent penetration test is done, or booked before or soon after launch.
criteria.evidence: Test report or booking.

checks.q: Is an independent penetration test done, or booked before or soon after launch?

criteria.title: The traffic target is agreed
criteria.standard: The target load is worked out from business numbers (visitors, time window, peak factor) and agreed: requests per second per endpoint and response-time budgets.
criteria.evidence: The worked target and who agreed it.

checks.q: Is the target load worked out from business numbers (visitors, time window, peak factor)?
Does it give requests per second per request type and response-time budgets?
Has a named person agreed it?

criteria.title: Load tested at and above target
criteria.standard: A stepped load test reaches at least 150% of target on a production-like setup, with results per step (rate achieved, p95 response time, errors).
criteria.evidence: Load test results.

checks.q: Was a stepped load test run up to at least 150% of the target, with results per step?
Did the app hold 150% of the target within its speed budgets and error limit?
Was it run on a production-like setup?

criteria.title: Load tests are repeated and kept
criteria.standard: The load test was run at least twice, and every run is kept, failures included.
criteria.evidence: All run results.

checks.q: Was the load test run at least twice?
Is every run kept, failures included?

criteria.title: Limited things survive a rush
criteria.standard: Stock, seats, coupons and balances survive many simultaneous buyers: never oversold, nobody charged twice.
criteria.evidence: A race test result.

checks.q: In a race test, was nothing sold beyond the stock?
In a race test, was nobody charged twice?

criteria.title: Slow partners are tested
criteria.standard: Behaviour is measured with the slowest realistic partner (payment, email, AI): responses of 3 to 10 seconds and time-outs cause no double actions and no pile-up.
criteria.evidence: A slow-partner test result.

checks.q: Was the slowest realistic partner simulated (answers of 3 to 10 seconds, and time-outs)?
Did that cause no double actions?
Did that cause no pile-up of waiting requests?

criteria.title: Hot paths are efficient
criteria.standard: Database queries on the busiest paths use indexes and no query-per-item loops. Hot reads are cached with a stated freshness.
criteria.evidence: Query plans or code review of the hot paths.

checks.q: Do the busiest paths avoid one-query-per-item loops and use indexes?
Are hot reads cached with a stated freshness?

criteria.title: Resources are bounded
criteria.standard: Connection pools, queues and request bodies have limits and time-outs. Work fails fast instead of waiting forever.
criteria.evidence: Configuration and code.

checks.q: Do connection pools and queues have limits and time-outs?
Do request bodies have a size limit?
Does work fail fast instead of waiting forever?

criteria.title: Overload is graceful
criteria.standard: Beyond capacity, the app sheds load (a queue page, 'try again', 429 or 503) instead of crashing or slowing everyone down.
criteria.evidence: A test beyond capacity.

checks.q: Beyond capacity, does the app turn people away politely (queue page, try again, 429 or 503) instead of crashing or slowing everyone down?

criteria.title: Pages are fast for people
criteria.standard: Key pages meet the Core Web Vitals 'good' thresholds on a mid-range phone.
criteria.evidence: Lighthouse or field data.

checks.q: Do key pages meet the Core Web Vitals 'good' thresholds on a mid-range phone profile?

criteria.title: Scaling is planned
criteria.standard: It is written down what to scale first, how quickly it can be scaled, and what peak costs.
criteria.evidence: The capacity plan.

checks.q: Is it written down what to scale first and how quickly?
Is the cost at peak written down?

criteria.title: Health checks are honest
criteria.standard: A liveness check (the process is up) and a readiness check (its dependencies answer) exist and expose nothing internal.
criteria.evidence: Calls to both, with a dependency down.

checks.q: Is there a liveness check?
Is there a readiness check that fails when a dependency is down?
Do the checks expose nothing internal?

criteria.title: Restarts and deploys are safe
criteria.standard: On shutdown the app finishes the requests in progress. A deploy or restart drops no requests and loses no data.
criteria.evidence: A restart under load.

checks.q: On shutdown, does the app finish the requests in progress?
Does a restart or deploy lose no data?

criteria.title: Backups restore
criteria.standard: Backups run automatically and a restore has been tried. Possible data loss is within the agreed limit.
criteria.evidence: Restore log.

checks.q: Do backups run automatically?
Was a restore tried, and did it work?
Is the possible data loss within the agreed limit?

criteria.title: Rollback works
criteria.standard: Going back to the previous release has been tried against the current database.
criteria.evidence: Rollback log.

checks.q: Was going back to the previous release tried against the current database, and did it work?

criteria.title: Problems reach a person
criteria.standard: Errors, response times and capacity are monitored, and alerts reach a named person who can act.
criteria.evidence: A test alert, received.
criteria.source: OWASP Top 10:2025 A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures

checks.q: Are errors, response times and capacity monitored?
Did a test alert reach a named person who can act?

criteria.title: Logs are useful and clean
criteria.standard: Logs are structured, carry a request id, and contain no secrets or personal data.
criteria.evidence: Logs from a test run.

checks.q: Are logs structured, with a request id?
Are logs free of secrets and personal data?

criteria.title: The runbook has been tried
criteria.standard: A launch and incident runbook exists, and every step was tried once with tools that exist.
criteria.evidence: The runbook and a rehearsal log.

checks.q: Is there a launch and incident runbook?
Was every step tried once, with tools that exist, and did it work?

criteria.title: Risky features can be paused
criteria.standard: Checkout, sign-up or a promotion can be paused without a deploy and without losing data.
criteria.evidence: Pause and resume, then compare data.

checks.q: Can checkout, sign-up or the promotion be paused without a deploy?
Is no data lost when it is paused and resumed?

criteria.title: Server settings fit the platform
criteria.standard: Keep-alive and time-out settings fit the load balancer, and request size limits are set.
criteria.evidence: Server and load balancer settings.

checks.q: Do keep-alive and time-out settings fit the load balancer?
Are request size limits set?

criteria.title: People are ready
criteria.standard: An on-call contact, an escalation path and a way to tell customers about problems are arranged for launch.
criteria.evidence: The rota and contact list.

checks.q: Is an on-call person named for the launch?
Is there an escalation path?
Is there a way to tell customers about problems?

criteria.title: Defect history is collected
criteria.standard: Defects from git history (fix commits, reverts), the issue tracker, incidents and earlier reviews are collected for the period under review.
criteria.evidence: History scan output and the sources used.

checks.q: Were fix commits and reverts collected from the git history?
Were the issue tracker, incident notes and earlier reviews collected, or their absence recorded?

criteria.title: Recurring problems are identified
criteria.standard: Defects are grouped into problem classes, and every class with two or more occurrences is listed.
criteria.evidence: The problem classes with their occurrences.

checks.q: Are the defects grouped into problem classes?
Is every class with two or more occurrences listed?

criteria.title: Root causes are named
criteria.standard: Each recurring class has a root cause that explains why it keeps happening (a design or process gap, not 'a typo'), found by reading the actual changes.
criteria.evidence: Root cause per class, with the commits or reports read.

checks.q: Does each recurring class have a root cause that explains why it keeps happening, found by reading the actual changes?

criteria.title: Controls prevent a repeat
criteria.standard: Each recurring class has a control that catches the next occurrence automatically: a test, a code-scanning rule, a database constraint, a type, a CI gate, or an agent rule backed by one of these.
criteria.evidence: The control, run against a known example.

checks.q: Does each recurring class have an automatic control (a test, a scanning rule, a constraint, a type or a CI gate)?
Was each control run against a known example and shown to catch it?

criteria.title: Fixes come with regression tests
criteria.standard: Each bug fix adds a test that fails without the fix.
criteria.evidence: A sample of fix commits.

checks.q: Does each bug fix in a sample of fix commits add a test that fails without the fix?

criteria.title: Hotspots are examined
criteria.standard: Files with the most fixes were reviewed in depth, and a refactor or extra tests are planned where needed.
criteria.evidence: Hotspot list and notes.

checks.q: Were the files with the most fixes reviewed in depth?
Is a refactor or extra tests planned where needed?

criteria.title: Known problems are registered
criteria.standard: Every open known problem is listed with severity, owner and due date.
criteria.evidence: The register.

checks.q: Is every open known problem listed with severity, owner and due date?

criteria.title: Fixes of fixes are explained
criteria.standard: Reverts and repeated fixes in the same place are explained, and their cause is covered by a control.
criteria.evidence: The reverts and repeat fixes, with notes.

checks.q: Are reverts and repeated fixes in one place explained?
Is their cause covered by a control?

criteria.title: The trend is measured
criteria.standard: Defects per problem class are compared with the previous review, to show the controls work.
criteria.evidence: Counts from both reviews.

checks.q: Are the defects per problem class compared with the previous review?

criteria.title: Criteria are agreed first
criteria.standard: Acceptance criteria are numbered, versioned and agreed by the product owner before testing. Changes are approved again.
criteria.evidence: The criteria file and its approvals.

checks.q: Are the acceptance criteria numbered and versioned?
Did the product owner agree them before testing?
Were later changes approved again?

criteria.title: Must criteria pass reliably
criteria.standard: Every Must criterion passes three runs in a row with no retries.
criteria.evidence: The acceptance run.

checks.q: Does every Must criterion pass three runs in a row with no retries?

criteria.title: Evidence can be seen
criteria.standard: User-visible behaviour has screenshots or recordings attached to each result.
criteria.evidence: The attachments.

checks.q: Does every user-visible result have a screenshot or recording attached?

criteria.title: Verdict first, in plain words
criteria.standard: The first screen of the report gives the verdict, the reason and the blockers in plain language.
criteria.evidence: The report.

checks.q: Does the report's first screen give the verdict, the reason and the blockers in plain language?

criteria.title: Every result is readable
criteria.standard: Each result has a plain-language impact. Numbers have units and the target beside them. Technical terms are in a glossary.
criteria.evidence: The report.

checks.q: Does each result have a plain-language impact?
Do numbers have units and the target beside them?
Are technical terms in a glossary?

criteria.title: Every claim links its evidence
criteria.standard: Each result links to its evidence, and whatever wasn't checked is listed.
criteria.evidence: The report.

checks.q: Does each result link to its evidence?
Is everything that wasn't checked listed?

criteria.title: The review can be repeated
criteria.standard: The report records the commit, date, tool versions and reviewer, so the review can be repeated.
criteria.evidence: The report.

checks.q: Does the report record the commit, date, tool versions and reviewer?

criteria.title: Key pages are accessible
criteria.standard: Key pages have no serious or critical accessibility violations in automated WCAG 2.1 AA checks.
criteria.evidence: Accessibility scan output.

checks.q: Do key pages have no serious or critical violations in automated WCAG 2.1 AA checks?

performanceTests.name: Load at the target and above it
performanceTests.proves: It holds the expected traffic, and shows where it breaks.

performanceTests.name: Repeated runs, all kept
performanceTests.proves: The same test run at least twice gives the same answer, and failed runs are kept too. Its result says whether the runs agreed.

performanceTests.name: Rush on something limited
performanceTests.proves: Many people buying or booking the last items at the same moment never oversell or pay twice.

performanceTests.name: Slow or failing partner
performanceTests.proves: When payment, email or an AI service is slow or down, nobody is charged twice or left stuck.

performanceTests.name: Beyond capacity
performanceTests.proves: Past its limit it turns people away politely and recovers, instead of crashing.

performanceTests.name: Long run
performanceTests.proves: An hour or more at normal traffic without slowing down, filling up or running out of memory.

performanceTests.name: Page speed on phones
performanceTests.proves: People on mid-range phones get the page quickly.

performanceTests.name: On a production-like setup
performanceTests.proves: The numbers hold on the real hosting, with a realistic amount of data, not only on a laptop.

hiddenIssueAreas.name: Two things at once
hiddenIssueAreas.look: Double clicks, two people taking the last item, a job running twice: anything that reads, decides and then writes.

hiddenIssueAreas.name: Slow, failing or repeated outside calls
hiddenIssueAreas.look: Every call to payment, email, AI or another service has a time limit and a repeat-safe key, and a time-out is treated as "unknown" and settled later, never as failed.

hiddenIssueAreas.name: Restarts, deploys and rollbacks
hiddenIssueAreas.look: What a restart or a new release does in the middle of a purchase: data that must survive, work that must finish, and going back to the previous version.

hiddenIssueAreas.name: Settings and environments
hiddenIssueAreas.look: A setting missing or wrong in production, the same setting in two places, test switches left on, test and live sharing data or keys.

hiddenIssueAreas.name: Unexpected input
hiddenIssueAreas.look: Malformed requests, huge bodies, odd characters and addresses: one bad request must not crash the app or corrupt data.

hiddenIssueAreas.name: What runs out first
hiddenIssueAreas.look: Connection pools, queues, memory, rate limits, a single server: what runs out first under load, and what happens then.

hiddenIssueAreas.name: Data that can become wrong
hiddenIssueAreas.look: Rules the data must obey (stock, money, one per customer) enforced where they cannot be bypassed: in the database or one transaction, not only on the screen.

hiddenIssueAreas.name: Time and dates
hiddenIssueAreas.look: Time zones, opening times, timers and schedules, dates typed by people, clocks that differ between machines.

hiddenIssueAreas.name: Background jobs and queues
hiddenIssueAreas.look: Jobs that retry, run twice, get stuck or fail silently: emails, settlements and clean-ups that never finish. With no jobs at all, look at the work that should be one (sending email or settling payments inside the request).

testKinds.name: Unit tests
testKinds.catches: A rule or calculation that is wrong: prices, limits, reading input, dates.

testKinds.name: Integration tests
testKinds.catches: Parts that work alone but not together: database rules and transactions, a stand-in payment provider that is slow or fails.

testKinds.name: End-to-end tests in a browser
testKinds.catches: A user journey that breaks: signing in, buying, seeing the order.

testKinds.name: Visual tests
testKinds.catches: A screen that looks wrong although it works: something that should disappear stays, things overlap, a layout breaks on a phone.

testKinds.name: Self-checks
testKinds.catches: The app checking itself: refusing to start with missing or unsafe settings, a health check that tests what matters, a quick test after every deploy.

testKinds.name: Load and race tests
testKinds.catches: Slow pages, overselling and double charges when many people arrive at once.

testKinds.name: Automatic scans
testKinds.catches: Leaked keys, risky code patterns, libraries with known security holes.

evidenceSources.name: The code, at the version inspected
evidenceSources.why: What is actually there, not what anyone remembers.

evidenceSources.name: Change history
evidenceSources.why: Fixes, reverts and the files that keep changing show what keeps going wrong.

evidenceSources.name: Issue tracker or tickets
evidenceSources.why: Bugs the team already knows about, and how often each kind came back.

evidenceSources.name: Reports from users and support
evidenceSources.why: Problems real people met, which tests did not.

evidenceSources.name: Earlier reviews and incident notes
evidenceSources.why: What was found before, and whether it was really fixed.

evidenceSources.name: The project's own tests, run again
evidenceSources.why: Whether they pass, and what they would never notice.

evidenceSources.name: The running app, used by the inspector
evidenceSources.why: What a user sees, including what tests skip.

evidenceSources.name: Load, race and speed measurements
evidenceSources.why: How it behaves under the expected traffic, measured rather than guessed.

evidenceSources.name: Automatic scans
evidenceSources.why: Leaked keys, risky patterns and vulnerable libraries, found by tools.

evidenceSources.name: Answers from the owner and the team
evidenceSources.why: The agreed requirements and the decisions behind the design.

toolbox.name: acceptance-test
toolbox.what: Turns what the owner expects into numbered criteria and browser tests with screenshots, run three times each; add Playwright screenshot comparisons for visual checks.

toolbox.name: peak-traffic-test
toolbox.what: Turns the expected crowd into a load plan, runs staged load tests and the race test, and explains the result in plain words.

toolbox.name: launch-review
toolbox.what: Runs the scanners and this inspection; its scanner script can run on every change in CI.

toolbox.name: webapp-testing
toolbox.what: Lets an AI agent drive a local web app in a real browser with Playwright: check behaviour, take screenshots, read the browser log.

toolbox.name: test-driven-development
toolbox.what: Makes the AI agent write a failing test before each fix or feature, so every bug fixed gets the test that stops it coming back.

toolbox.name: systematic-debugging
toolbox.what: Makes the AI agent find the root cause of a bug before changing code, instead of patching the symptom.

toolbox.name: verification-before-completion
toolbox.what: Makes the AI agent prove a fix works (run the test, show the output) before it says the work is done.

toolbox.name: Playwright screenshot comparison
toolbox.what: Compares each screen with an approved picture and fails when it changes; the usual way to add visual tests to browser tests.
